body:
The Earth as a layered planet

The Earth is a dynamic planet whose internal processes continuously influence its surface. Mountain building, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and the movement of continents are closely connected with the structure and physical conditions of its interior.

The Earth has a mean radius of approximately 6,371 km. Its materials are arranged in distinct layers because, during its early evolution, heavier materials such as iron became concentrated towards the centre, while relatively lighter rocky materials formed the outer layers. This separation of materials according to their physical and chemical properties is called differentiation.

On the basis of chemical composition, the Earth is divided into 3 principal layers: the crust, mantle and core.

Crust

The crust is the outermost and thinnest compositional layer of the Earth. It consists of solid rocks and forms both the continents and the ocean floors. Its thickness and composition are not uniform.

Continental and oceanic crust

FeatureContinental crustOceanic crust
Typical thickness30–40 km5–10 km
Representative rockGraniteBasalt
Approximate density2.7 g/cm33.0 g/cm3
Traditional termSialSima
General ageIncludes very ancient rocksGenerally much younger

Continental crust is particularly thick beneath major mountain systems. Beneath the Himalayas, its thickness may reach approximately 70 km.

The traditional term Sial refers to material relatively rich in silica and aluminium or alumina, while Sima refers to material relatively rich in silica and magnesium. These terms are simplified descriptions of crustal composition, not two universally continuous layers.

Oceanic crust is thinner but denser than continental crust. This difference is important in understanding why oceanic lithosphere generally descends beneath continental lithosphere when they converge.

Mantle

The mantle extends from the base of the crust to a depth of approximately 2,900 km. It is the largest of the 3 principal compositional layers by volume.

The mantle consists mainly of silicate minerals rich in magnesium and iron. Although its temperature is very high, most of the mantle remains solid. Under sustained forces over geological time, mantle rocks can deform and flow extremely slowly.

The mantle is broadly divided into the upper mantle and lower mantle. Some parts of the upper mantle provide the material from which magma is generated. This does not mean that the entire upper mantle is molten.

Core

The core extends from a depth of approximately 2,900 km to the Earth's centre. It consists predominantly of iron, together with nickel and smaller quantities of lighter elements. Its traditional name is Nife, derived from Ni for nickel and Fe for iron.

  • Outer core: Extends from approximately 2,900 km to 5,150 km below the surface. It is liquid.
  • Inner core: Extends from approximately 5,150 km to the centre of the Earth at 6,371 km. It is solid.

The inner core has a higher temperature than the outer core, but enormous pressure keeps its material solid. Movement of electrically conducting liquid metal in the outer core is responsible for generating the Earth's main magnetic field.

Major internal discontinuities

A seismic discontinuity is a boundary across which the speed or behaviour of seismic waves changes markedly because the properties of the surrounding material change.

DiscontinuitySeparatesApproximate depth
Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)Crust and mantleVaries with crustal thickness
Gutenberg discontinuityMantle and outer core2,900 km
Lehmann discontinuityOuter core and inner core5,150 km

Physical state of the interior

The crust, most of the mantle and the inner core are solid. The outer core is liquid. High temperature alone does not determine whether a material is solid or liquid; pressure also matters.

Prelims focus

  • The crust is the thinnest compositional layer; the mantle is the largest by volume.
  • Continental crust is generally thicker and less dense than oceanic crust.
  • The mantle-core boundary lies at approximately 2,900 km.
  • Moho separates the crust and mantle; Gutenberg separates the mantle and core.
  • Nife refers to the iron-nickel composition of the core.
  • Trap: The inner core is solid even though it is hotter than the liquid outer core.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 2, pp. 7–8; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 3, pp. 22–23; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 18–20; IGNOU, BGYCL-132 Practical Manual, Experiment 1, Section 1.3.2; NASA, Earth Fact Sheet, Bulk Parameters; USGS, Are the Tectonic Plates Floating on Magma? Online sources consulted 27 November 2026. Readable online textbook copies supplement the partly unreadable project-library scans.]

title: Structure and Composition of the Earth's Interior

body:
Conditions below the Earth's surface

Temperature, pressure and density generally increase towards the Earth's interior. Together, these properties determine the physical behaviour of rocks and metals at different depths.

Temperature and the geothermal gradient

The rate at which temperature increases with depth is known as the geothermal gradient. The rate varies from one region to another and is not constant throughout the Earth.

Near the surface, measurements in mines and boreholes show an increase in temperature with depth. However, this near-surface rate cannot be extended uniformly to the Earth's centre because different internal layers transfer heat differently.

The Earth possesses internal heat mainly because of 2 sources:

  • Residual heat: Heat retained from the Earth's formation and early differentiation.
  • Radiogenic heat: Heat released by the natural radioactive decay of elements such as uranium, thorium and potassium.

Pressure and density

Pressure increases with depth because the material at a given level supports the weight of the overlying layers. Increasing pressure compresses materials and can raise their melting temperature.

The Earth's mean density is approximately 5.5 g/cm3, considerably higher than the density of typical continental crust, approximately 2.7 g/cm3. This difference supports the conclusion that the deeper interior contains much denser materials.

The distribution of heavier elements towards the core and the compression of material under high pressure both contribute to increasing density towards the centre.

Lithosphere and asthenosphere

While the terms crust, mantle and core classify the Earth primarily according to composition, the terms lithosphere and asthenosphere classify its outer region according to mechanical behaviour.

Lithosphere

The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell of the Earth. It includes the entire crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle.

It is broken into several large and small tectonic plates. These plates move as relatively rigid units over the weaker mantle beneath them.

Lithospheric thickness varies with location and geological history. Newly formed oceanic lithosphere is relatively thin, while old continental lithosphere can be considerably thicker.

Asthenosphere

The asthenosphere is a mechanically weak region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. Its rocks are predominantly solid but sufficiently hot and deformable to flow slowly over geological time.

Some regions contain small quantities of partially molten material. Its relatively weak nature permits the movement of the rigid lithospheric plates above it.

In simplified school-level descriptions, the asthenosphere is considered to extend to a depth of approximately 400 km. Its actual boundaries and thickness are variable.

Crust is not the same as lithosphere

The crust is a compositional layer. The lithosphere is a mechanical layer that includes both the crust and a portion of the upper mantle. The asthenosphere is part of the upper mantle, not part of the core.

Mantle convection and plate movement

Internal heat produces temperature and density differences within the mantle. Relatively hotter, less dense mantle material tends to rise, while cooler, denser material tends to descend. This slow circulation contributes to the transfer of heat through the mantle and the movement of tectonic plates.

Arthur Holmes proposed the importance of mantle convection in explaining continental movement during the early development of modern tectonic theory.

Plate movement is also influenced by gravity-related forces:

  • Slab pull: Cold, dense oceanic lithosphere sinks into the mantle and helps pull the remaining plate towards a subduction zone.
  • Ridge push: Gravity contributes to the movement of lithosphere away from elevated mid-oceanic ridges.

Tectonic plates commonly move at rates measured in centimetres per year. Such movements appear insignificant over a human lifetime but can rearrange entire continents over millions of years.

Prelims focus

  • Temperature and pressure generally increase with depth.
  • Geothermal gradient is the increase in temperature per unit depth.
  • The lithosphere includes the crust and rigid uppermost mantle.
  • The asthenosphere is a weak, predominantly solid region of the upper mantle.
  • Internal heat, mantle convection and gravity-related forces contribute to plate movement.
  • Trap: Tectonic plates do not float on a worldwide ocean of molten magma.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 18–20; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapters 3–4, pp. 22–23, 28 and 33–34; NASA, Earth Fact Sheet, Bulk Parameters; USGS, Are the Tectonic Plates Floating on Magma?; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Some Unanswered Questions. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Temperature, Pressure and the Mechanical Layers of the Earth

body:
Why indirect evidence is necessary

Scientists cannot directly observe most of the Earth's interior. The depths reached through mining and scientific drilling are extremely small compared with the Earth's mean radius of approximately 6,371 km.

Knowledge of the deeper interior therefore depends on combining direct observations of accessible materials with indirect physical evidence.

Direct sources

Direct sources provide actual geological materials that can be collected, observed or analysed.

  • Surface rocks: Exposed rocks provide information about the composition and geological history of accessible parts of the crust.
  • Mining: Mines expose rocks beneath the Earth's surface and allow measurements of temperature and other physical conditions at depth.
  • Scientific drilling: Boreholes provide rock samples and measurements from deeper portions of the crust. The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reached a depth of approximately 12 km.
  • Volcanic materials: Lava, gases and rock fragments brought to the surface during eruptions provide information about their source materials and internal geological processes.

Volcanic eruptions do not provide direct access to the Earth's core. Magma may also undergo chemical and physical changes during its movement towards the surface, so erupted material must be interpreted carefully.

Indirect sources

Density and gravity

The Earth's average density is greater than that of its surface rocks, indicating that denser materials exist inside it. Measurements of the Earth's gravitational field also reveal differences in the distribution of mass.

A gravity anomaly is a difference between an observed gravity value and the value expected after accounting for relevant reference conditions. Such differences help scientists identify variations in the density and distribution of subsurface materials.

Magnetic evidence

Magnetic measurements provide information about magnetic minerals and structures in the crust. The existence and behaviour of the Earth's main magnetic field also support the presence of moving, electrically conducting material within its outer core.

Meteorites

Meteorites are solid extraterrestrial materials that reach the Earth's surface. Some contain substantial quantities of iron and nickel. Because meteorites and the Earth originated from materials associated with the early Solar System, studying them helps scientists understand the possible composition of planetary interiors.

Meteorites are indirect evidence: they are not samples extracted from the Earth's core.

Seismic evidence

Earthquakes generate waves that travel through the Earth. Their speeds, paths, arrival times and disappearance from particular regions reveal changes in the composition and physical state of internal materials.

Seismic waves are particularly valuable because they can travel through regions far beyond the reach of mines and boreholes. They provide the principal evidence for identifying the Earth's internal boundaries and determining that the outer core is liquid.

Most important evidence

Seismic evidence provides the most detailed information about the layered structure and physical state of the deep Earth. Direct geological samples are important but are restricted to accessible materials.

Prelims focus

  • Mining, drilling and volcanic materials are direct sources of geological information.
  • Gravity, magnetic observations, meteorites and seismic waves provide indirect evidence.
  • The Kola Superdeep Borehole is located in Russia and reached approximately 12 km.
  • Gravity anomalies help identify differences in subsurface mass distribution.
  • Trap: Meteorites provide clues about core composition but are not actual samples of the Earth's core.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 3, pp. 18–20; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 18–19; USGS, The Interior of the Earth, Core and Mantle sections. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
